blocks.heading: From game jam to vertical slice
blocks.body:
Lightkeeper began as Fell Out, a game-jam project about exploring a fog-covered archipelago and meeting its inhabitants.

Concept funding from FFF Bayern in 2024 gave us room to develop the pitch and test a larger world. Prototype funding followed later that year. We explored traversal, gathering, progression, and character interaction, then narrowed the scope to reach a playable vertical slice.

blocks.heading: Design and production scope
blocks.body: I worked on game design, UI/UX, progression, level design, map layouts, prototyping, and production. The wider vertical-slice work also involved writing, world building, content creation, and marketing, from the pitch deck and game-design documentation through the playable slice.

blocks.heading: Tools for world building
blocks.body: Terrain, progression, and layout tools supported the team’s work on world scale, pacing, and content. The demonstrations show how those authoring workflows connect to the playable game.

blocks.heading: Before the vertical slice
blocks.body: The technical test was where we searched for visual direction, world scale and traversal before committing to the current slice.

blocks.heading: Fell out
blocks.body: The game-jam idea became a formal high-concept pitch and received EUR 20,000 in concept funding from FFF Bayern in 2024.

blocks.heading: What changed
blocks.body: We expanded systems before proving the core loop. Later changes in direction meant cutting completed survival, farming, building, and content work. Those cuts made the relationship between scope and the core experience a central production question.

title: LIGHTKEEPER.GAME
heading: Lightkeeper
description: An exploration game built around traversal, discovery, and character encounters across a fog-covered archipelago. I led game design and production through a playable vertical slice.

blocks.heading: Designing the investigation
blocks.body:
KERN is in development. My focus is how a player investigates an unfamiliar anomaly: observing its behavior, testing an explanation, and choosing what to do next.

I design and prototype gameplay systems, tools, and interfaces directly in-engine, iterating interaction details through hands-on use. The mechanics and world identity are developed together so the fiction supports the investigation. The footage shows prototypes and experiments, not a finished game.

blocks.heading: Evidence, not checklists
blocks.body: The design goal is for tools to reveal evidence the player can interpret. An encounter should preserve uncertainty and risk, while an explanation should lead to an action rather than only a label.

blocks.heading: An institution inside the world
blocks.body: The identity belongs to an organization operating inside the Zone. Its graphics are part of the setting and the way the player encounters information.

blocks.heading: Questions still being tested
blocks.body: I am testing how much uncertainty an investigation can support, how tools should overlap, and what should persist after an encounter.

title: KERN.GAME
heading: KERN
description: Designing an investigation game in which players observe anomalies, test their ideas with tools, and act on what they learn.

blocks.heading: Connecting a multidisciplinary production
blocks.body:
Dronies required a consistent direction across collection art, product, web, story, comics, merchandise, and launch creative. I worked as creative director, art director, and producer across the project.

My work combined hands-on design with communication between artists, designers, developers, marketing, community, operations, and external partners. That included coordination with the Solana Labs team around the partnership.

The work was collaborative. My contribution was setting direction, producing key pieces, and coordinating the disciplines and people involved.

blocks.heading: Scope and launch
blocks.body:
I led day-to-day production across nine design and development teams involving roughly 30 contributors, coordinating priorities and delivery with Solana Labs and planning the marketing campaign.

The official collection contained 10,000 pieces and sold out in five minutes. The project generated approximately US$3M in sales.

blocks.heading: Keeping everyday editing predictable
blocks.body:
Repeated scene-editing tasks can interrupt the work when transforms, panels, or selection behavior are difficult to predict. For KERN, my co-founder and I are modifying the Flax editor around the interactions we use throughout the day.

I work on editor UX and engine-fork changes across transforms, hierarchy, properties, docking, navigation, and content browsing. The aim is to preserve context, make feedback precise, and reduce avoidable interruptions while building the game.

blocks.heading: Interaction goals
blocks.body: Keep handles predictable, preserve mode and focus, show the correct axes, and make the result of each action clear.

blocks.heading: Implementation status
blocks.body: I redesign and implement editor UI, workflows, and interface feedback for the Flax game engine, with selected changes contributed upstream. This case also includes experiments in our engine fork; those fork-only changes are not official Flax features.

heading: Flax editor workflows

blocks.heading: Making Daedalus Alpha
blocks.body:
Daedalus Alpha is a seven-minute live-action short about a scientist confronting an apparent superintelligence. I developed the concept over several months, then produced, directed, and edited the film.

The production involved nine crew members, including me, and three cast members. We shot overnight, from roughly 8 PM to 8 AM. Directing performances while coordinating the production made the practical demands of the story much clearer.

blocks.heading: Building a coherent narrative world
blocks.body:
Daedalus began as Estafos & Suraya: a test of whether a small team could turn generated source imagery into a coherent narrative project.

I wrote the story and built the world, generated 9,000 source images, and selected and edited the material into a 12-page comic. I assembled the layouts in Figma, animated 12 panels in Rive, and helped build an interactive web reader with a licensed soundtrack. The world expanded into a website, brand, merchandise, and live-action film work with collaborators.

blocks.heading: From script to reader
blocks.body: The process moved from story and script to source-image selection and cleanup, page design in Figma, panel animation in Rive, and a reader state machine with JavaScript progression. The central challenge was maintaining continuity across inconsistent source material.

blocks.heading: How I introduced the project
blocks.body:
A process-led post reached 9K views. A later post about the personal reason for making the comic reached 2.0M views, 3,417 upvotes, and 236 comments. These were different posts, not a controlled comparison.

The contrast changed how I introduced the work: personal motivation first, production process second.

blocks.heading: A conversation with superintelligence

I wrote and pitched the film, then worked as producer, director, and editor, coordinating the 12-person production from planning through the shoot and final delivery.

blocks.heading: An overnight production
blocks.body: The production involved nine crew members, including me, and three cast members. We shot from roughly 8 PM to 8 AM. I directed performances, coordinated departments, responded to practical constraints on set, and shaped the final film in the edit.

blocks.heading: White Mirror
blocks.body: The film was made for White Mirror, an anthology initiative produced by CHAPTR and The Culture DAO around human-machine collaboration. The initiative was presented in a Venice Production Bridge session at the 80th Venice International Film Festival in 2023, moderated by Edward Saatchi of Fable Simulation and Philipp Nastaly of CHAPTR. That presentation does not establish that Daedalus Alpha itself screened at the festival.

blocks.heading: The fantasy worked. the loop did not.
blocks.body:
Void Overdrive began as a single-player hoverbike prototype and quickly became a multiplayer test bed for an open world. We rebuilt the hoverbike and networking stack in Unreal as well as Unity to understand the tradeoffs between engines; Unity ultimately gave us a stronger path for moment-to-moment gameplay.

The unresolved problem was the game itself. Fast traversal and the pleasure of exploring a huge landscape pulled toward immediate action, while the experience we wanted—maintenance, costly pursuit and slow, methodical survival—pulled the other way. We did not find a gameplay loop that reconciled those two experiences. That tension is the most useful part of the project now.

description: Tested whether fast hoverbike exploration could support a slower survival game. The prototype exposed an unresolved conflict between those two experiences.

blocks.heading: Atmosphere as the primary mechanic
blocks.body:
Project Hypno was our first attempt at a horror game. I wrote the script in a week and we developed the prototype around the kind of deep, tactile simulation we loved in Voices of the Void, searching for a player fantasy that could support those mechanics rather than simply copying their surface.

The two-week project pushed me into unfamiliar territory: modeling, PBR materials, spatial sound design and the pacing of a horror atmosphere. It proved that we could create the mood, but not yet the larger gameplay framework that would sustain it.

blocks.heading: One week, one song, one world
blocks.body: I had been carrying this world around in my head for months, then gave myself one week to make it visible. I used a single song as the spine and pushed my Blender skills through every scene I could finish in that window. Mannequins kept character work outside the scope so I could focus on the environments and presentation.

blocks.heading: Reconsidering the presentation
blocks.body:
Mighty Pebble tested a clicker in which a small god gathers resources and buys upgrades that change the world’s output. I built the prototype in 3D.

Comparisons with Clicky Islands and Clickyland made me want to test a 2D presentation for clearer, more immediate interactions. That reflection changed how I think about presentation and scope on future projects.

blocks.heading: From mud to an empire
blocks.body:
Mattercraft asks what happens when a card game and clicker economy are combined with Little Alchemy. You begin with soil and mud, combine tools and materials, and gradually build a production system. The prototype made the crafting readable, but its only pressure came from managing an increasingly crowded field of cards.

In hindsight, it needed pushback: rats entering the system, furnaces consuming wood, cutters feeding tree production and relationships that gradually become a Factorio-like visual program. That missing pressure is the part I would explore if I return to it.

description: A card-based crafting prototype combining material recipes and a clicker economy, with automation as a direction for further development.

blocks.heading: One week, a lot of feedback
blocks.body:
Spacekeeper was built in a week using Bezi AI to test how quickly AI-assisted development could turn an idea into something playable. The concept mixed space management with gathering and survival, wrapped in the readable daily rhythm of Stardew Valley.

The most valuable work was the feedback layer: UI response, in-world response, sound and the small feedback details that make an unfinished system feel legible. The core loop was still too weak for the scope the idea demanded, so we stopped at the prototype.

blocks.heading: Separating the trailer from the game
blocks.body:
Fox Stories presented a cozy adventure, but the implemented prototype was much smaller. Players could explore and pick up items; the trailer’s NPC interactions were scripted. Stealing, progression, and a sustained gameplay loop were not implemented.

The response to the trailer outpaced the game. It pushed us to ask what the player actually does and how that role connects them to the world.

blocks.heading: The fantasy traveled further than the prototype
blocks.body: The response was exciting, but it exposed the gap between a world people wanted and a game we knew how to make. I keep the number here as evidence of resonance, not as proof that the design was solved.

blocks.heading: My first game, made in one week
Learning by shipping
blocks.body:
Moving On Express was my first game and my first time using Unity, Bolt and MagicaVoxel. I built almost everything—from the game design and voxel assets to the mechanical and technical implementation—in one week. The soundtrack was created by CillianCreates.

You play a mover loading a family’s belongings into a truck under a time limit. Speed matters, but damaged property comes out of your paycheck. It is a small idea, but shipping it taught me more than another month of abstract preparation would have.

blocks.heading: Plan the day, not the entire universe
blocks.body:
Yesterday starts with a drawer containing everything you could do, then asks you to choose what actually belongs today. Tasks can be organized into Must Do, Communications and general lists, placed into scheduled work blocks, and rolled forward when unfinished. Reflection, due dates, theme controls and dense keyboard navigation are part of the same idea: make daily planning more honest without turning it into another management job.

The desktop app is built with Electron, React and TypeScript and runs on Windows and macOS.

blocks.heading: Chords without breaking flow
blocks.body: MIDI Clip Builder is designed for learning and composing with chords quickly from the keyboard. A single note can become a chord, and the tool adjusts the result as you move between keys, chord systems and progressions. The aim is to make harmonic relationships easier to explore through use.

blocks.heading: A sound library that understands its folders
blocks.body:
Sonilabs indexes large local sound libraries and makes them searchable by filename, metadata, folder, format, tags and source. Sounds can be previewed against a waveform, adjusted for gain, trimmed to a selected region and queued for export without leaving the library. Manual tags and notes sit beside the structure already present in filenames and folders.

The app is local-first and built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, Rust and SQLite. Audio, cache data, analysis and export jobs stay on the machine.

title: SONILABS.APP
heading: Sonilabs
description: Built a local sound-library workflow for finding, previewing, trimming, and exporting audio without switching between separate tools.

blocks.heading: The part between a screen recording and a shareable clip
blocks.body:
QuickClipper is a focused desktop clip editor for the repetitive work that happens after capturing a screen recording: choose the useful region, set in and out points, crop or resize the frame, keep the export under a file-size target, and get the result out quickly. The interface keeps the source pool, viewer, inspector and timeline visible at once so a small edit does not grow into a full editing session.

The current app is built with Tauri and React. It produces Windows installers, supports signed GitHub releases and updates, and includes video, audio and audio-only export paths.

title: CLIPPER.APP
heading: QuickClipper
description: Built a desktop tool for the work between a screen recording and a shareable clip: trimming, reframing, setting a file-size target, and exporting.

title: BAD_JUPITER.PRODUCT
heading: Bad Jupiter
description: Designed chatbot and web-app onboarding, flows, and interfaces, taking user research into interactive prototypes and supporting a Product Hunt launch.

blocks.heading: From research to onboarding
blocks.body: I researched users and developed personas, then produced onboarding flows, wireframes, and high-fidelity mockups for Bad Jupiter’s chatbot and web application. I used Figma and Framer to prototype the interactions and supported the Product Hunt launch.

title: IDEA_RANCH.WEB
heading: Idea Ranch web design and development
description: Designed and developed brand websites, connecting information architecture, interaction flows, visual design, and implementation.

blocks.heading: Brand websites from structure to implementation
blocks.body:
At Idea Ranch I designed and developed websites for brands including Toyota, Remington, Christie Cookies Co, and Carhartt. I translated requirements into information architecture, interaction flows, visual design, and working web pages.

The work included wireframes and designs in Sketch and Photoshop, UX documentation for design and development teams, and information-architecture documents for large websites.

title: MERCK.PRODUCT
heading: Merck product design
description: Product strategy, UX concepts, interaction design, and design-system work for a healthcare client through Unfold.

blocks.heading: Engagement summary
blocks.body: My work at Unfold included product strategy, UX concepts, interaction design, and design systems for Merck, as part of the team’s healthcare client work.
